business_model.basis: Stated in P1 (20-F Item 4 Business Overview).
business_model.claim: IHS Towers is one of the largest independent owners, operators and developers of shared communications infrastructure in the world, providing critical infrastructure to MNOs and other customers in emerging markets across two regions and seven countries, serving approximately 647 million people.
quotes: We are one of the largest independent owners, operators and developers of shared communications infrastructure in the world, providing our customers, most of whom are leading MNOs, with critical infrastructure that facilitates mobile communications coverage and connectivity for approximately 647 million people in emerging markets, across two regions and seven countries.

business_model.basis: Stated in P1 (Business Overview) and P3 (Item 5 Operating Results).
business_model.claim: Revenue is generated through three service categories: Colocation (adding new tenants to existing towers), Lease Amendments (adding equipment or ancillary services at existing sites), and New Sites (constructing new towers to customer specifications).
quotes: We provide our customers with opportunities to lease space on existing Towers alongside current Tenants, known as Colocation, to install additional equipment on a Tower or request certain ancillary services, known as Lease Amendments, or to commission the construction of new Towers to the customer's specifications, known as New Sites.
Colocation and Lease Amendments are key drivers of incremental organic revenue in communications infrastructure sharing.

business_model.claim: The company reports three operating segments: Nigeria; Sub Saharan Africa (SSA, comprising Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, South Africa, Zambia and until October 9, 2025 Rwanda); and Latin America (Latam, comprising Brazil and Colombia), with Latam reclassified as a discontinued operation.
quotes: Our three operating segments are Nigeria, which comprises our operations in Nigeria; Sub Saharan Africa, or SSA, which comprises our operations in Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, South Africa, Zambia (and, until October 9, 2025, Rwanda); and Latin America, or Latam, which comprises our operations in Brazil and Colombia. Latam became a discontinued operation but it continues to be reported to our CODM as a segment.

business_model.claim: Revenue is highly concentrated: for 2025 and 2024, the top three MNO customers in each individual market collectively accounted for 99% of consolidated revenue, and 68% of 2025 revenue from continuing operations came from Nigerian operations.
quotes: for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024, revenue from our top three MNO customers, considered in each of our individual markets of operation, collectively accounted for 99% and 99%, respectively, of our consolidated revenue.
a significant portion of our revenue is currently derived from our Nigerian operations (68% of our revenue from continuing operations, for the year ended December 31, 2025)

business_model.claim: The company typically enters into long-term Master Lease Agreements (MLAs) of 5 to 10 years, which include annual or semi-annual inflation-linked revenue escalators and, in certain cases, periodic foreign exchange reset mechanisms to adjust for local currency devaluation.
quotes: we typically enter into long-term MLAs of 5 to 10 years in duration, which have historically yielded strong renewal rates

Our MLAs typically include annual or semi-annual inflation-linked revenue escalators, limited customer termination rights and, in certain cases, provisions designed to help mitigate foreign exchange risk, such periodic reset mechanisms to adjust for local currency devaluation.

business_model.claim: In 2025, 47% of revenue from continuing operations was linked to the U.S. dollar and euro, and 23% was linked to power indexation and power pass-through.
quotes: For the years ended December 31, 2025, 2024 and 2023, 47%, 52% and 55%, respectively, of our revenue from continuing operations was linked to the U.S. dollar and euro.
For the years ended December 31, 2025, 2024, and 2023, 23% , 16%, and 11%, respectively, of our revenue from continuing operations was linked to power indexation and power pass-through.

business_model.claim: The company also provides fiber connectivity: Fiber-to-the-Tower (FTTT) in Nigeria and Fiber-to-the-Home (FTTH) in Brazil through I-Systems, as well as in-building solutions / distributed antenna systems (DAS) and Managed Services (maintenance, security, power supply for third-party towers).
quotes: Additionally, in Nigeria we provide "Fiber-to-the-Tower" or "FTTT" connectivity to our customers, while in Brazil, through I-Systems, we provide "Fiber-to-the-Home" or "FTTH" fiber connectivity to our customers through a neutral network infrastructure solution for broadband service

Finally, we lease space to our customers in secure locations within large building complexes, such as shopping malls, stadiums and airports, which we refer to as in-building solutions or distributed antenna systems ("DAS"). In certain strategic instances, we may also provide Managed Services, such as maintenance, security and power supply for Towers owned by third parties.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated explicitly in P3 as a key driver; the 1.46x colocation rate and tenant count are reported figures in P1 and P3.
growth_thesis.claim: Colocation and Lease Amendments on existing towers are the primary driver of incremental organic revenue, supported by a Colocation Rate of only 1.46x across 54,874 Tenants, indicating substantial unused capacity.
quotes: Colocation and Lease Amendments are key drivers of incremental organic revenue in communications infrastructure sharing.
As of December 31, 2025, our owned and operated tower portfolio supported 54,874 Tenants, with a Colocation Rate of 1.46x.
the main incremental cost to deliver Colocation or Lease Amendments is between $5,000 and $10,000 in augmentation capital expenditure, and from $10,000 to $12,000 in our Latin America business.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P3 as a key driver; cost ranges are company estimates; the no-speculative-building policy is a stated constraint.
growth_thesis.claim: New Site construction is a secondary organic growth driver, with the company building only after securing a long-term lease commitment, at an average cost of $50,000–$100,000 per site in Africa.
quotes: New Site construction is a key driver of incremental organic revenue through the customer revenue we invoice from the date the New Site becomes ready for service.

The average cost to build a New Site in our African markets is typically in the range of between $50,000 and $100,000, while in Latin America the cost is typically in the range of between $40,000 and $80,000 depending on the market of operation and specification of the tower.

We do not engage in speculative building and only construct New Sites after obtaining a commitment for a long-term lease with an initial tenant, and, in general, if we are aware of, or believe that there is, commercial potential for Colocation.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P3 as a structural feature of MLAs; the percentage figures are reported in P1.

quotes: Our MLAs generally contain inflation-linked escalation provisions under which the underlying lease fees, and therefore our revenue, may increase each year.
For the years ended December 31, 2025, 2024 and 2023, 47%, 52% and 55%, respectively, of our revenue from continuing operations was linked to the U.S. dollar and euro.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P2 and P3 as a contractual mechanism; the 68% Nigeria concentration is reported in P2; the 64.4% Naira depreciation figure is in P2.

Such MLAs typically have U.S. dollar-denominated components and local currency components of pricing, and the U.S. dollar components are converted to the local currency for settlement at a fixed conversion rate for a stated period of time, which conversion rates are reset monthly or quarterly.
